title: The Celestin Columbia record and Tuxedo band personnel
summary: He lists musicians on the record, explains he was hired just for it, and describes early drum sets.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Do you remember us was on that recording, Dave? Can you remember that?

Who was on that recording? Yeah, can you remember that? Let me see, yeah, I might have seen it now. It was... Let me see. John, it was John Murray. It was the Tuxedo band, but it was John's record. I had numbers. I think he had... Let me see. Now, he had Bill Matthew, trombone. He didn't use record. I think he had these... He wanted me on drum. He had... I think he had Jeanette. Let me see. I think Jeanette's playing piano. And Paul Bones. Sam Segarra. He didn't have the song. Sam Segarra, I think, was playing Sousa for him. Did you notice there was a bass horn effect on it? I think he had Sam Segarra. 된 stuff with
It was on trumpets. Can you remember the trumpets?
I think it was Rickard and Celestine. Oh, yeah. Let's see. I think it was Rickard. Alexa, remember Rickard?
Oh, sure, yeah.
Rickard and Celestine was playing trumpets. We were ready. I got eight minutes to make that.
You were working regular with that band?
No, not the young tuxedo band.
Oh, and they just got you for the record?
Yes, for the record. See, yeah, this play there.
Who was there using regular?
Johnny Bebe. Abbey for Johnny. Oh, yeah.
How come the Johnny wasn't on the record?
Well, you see, sometimes fellas them days, they make, a man might make, he can pick men's out of different bands to record. You could do that. And that label still was on the tuxedo band.
Yeah.
As long as you manage of a band be there, fellas can place the men's he wanted, you see.
So that wasn't an actual working band then, that record?

Yeah, that record, yeah, it was a tuxedo band, but excepting me, I was a member of the young tuxedo band, but I was considered a member of that band because most of the time, if Johnny wouldn't make a job, I'd work with that band, you see.
Yeah, yeah. Well, remember a Chinese woman, now we got onto him. Can you remember what he used to play like?

Johnny. The regular drum set, you know, you had the small tombs. All drums, they consisted of a hi-hat, or either a flow sax symbol, a symbol on the side of the bass, four cowbells or two on the chani, but one cry symbol, that's all, you know. All drummers used that, them days. They didn't have the big tunable tombs like you got, started in the late, I think the late 20s, early 30s like that, the tunable tombs.
They had those Chinese tombs, did they?

Yeah. The small ones, yeah. Yeah. But some of them be 60s, yeah, on the side of your bass. Yeah. And you could, you know, there's kind of, had a different effect in these tunable tombs that's what they did with these keys rings. Yeah.
They come out around, I believe, the other part of the 30s, them tunable tombs.
